\end{gathered}\tag{GSR1}
\]
The original $h$, $v_h=(2\xi)/h$, complete Taylor unit,
remainder map $J_{\chi,N}$ and observation $\Lambda$ are the
unchanged ones of GCR1--GCR2 and GCR41--GCR44.
Let
\[
 N_0=q-1,\quad N_1=q,\quad N_2=2q-1,\quad N_3=2q,
 \qquad(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3)=(1,1,-1,-1).
\]
The object calculated below is precisely
$\mathfrak T_k=\sum_a\epsilon_a
(\log\det G_{N_a}^0-\log\det G_{N_a}^\sigma)$
from GCR26. No source mass or packet coordinate is changed.

\subsection{The two exact low endpoints}

Use the full source determinant product and source bound
\[
\begin{gathered}
 D_{l,N}=\prod_{a=0}^N\prod_{r=0}^{2l-1}(a+r+\tfrac12),\qquad
 \mathscr U_{l,N}=\prod_{j=0}^{l-1}
                         \bigl(4(N+j+1)^2+t_j^2\bigr),\\
 X_{l,N}=(N+1)\log\mathscr U_{l,N}-\log D_{l,N}\geq0.
\end{gathered}\tag{GSR2}
\]
These are exactly GCR28--GCR30. Put
$A_N=\log\det G_N^f-\log\det G_N^\sigma$, where $G_N^0=\beta_kG_N^f$.
For $N\geq q-1$ let
\[
 r_N=N+1-q,\qquad
 R_N=
 \frac{\det\operatorname{Gram}_\sigma
                 (f\chi,f\chi S,\ldots,f\chi S^{r_N-1})}
      {\det\operatorname{Gram}_\sigma
                 (\chi,\chi S,\ldots,\chi S^{r_N-1})}.
\tag{GSR3}
\]
Both empty determinants at $r_N=0$ are one. GCR19 proves
the exact identity
\[
 A_N=\log D_{l,N}-\log R_N.
\tag{GSR4}
\]
In particular, define the full original moment ratio
\[
 \mathfrak r_\chi=
 \frac{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb R}
              |f(c+iy)\chi(c+iy)|^2\,d\sigma(y)}
      {\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb R}
              |\chi(c+iy)|^2\,d\sigma(y)}>0.
\tag{GSR5}
\]
Then
\[
 A_{q-1}=\log D_{l,q-1},\qquad
 A_q=\log D_{l,q}-\log\mathfrak r_\chi.
\tag{GSR6}
\]
The first source has no relation directions and the second
has the single original direction $\chi$. This is an equality,
not an estimate which treats either kernel as having growing rank.
All moments are finite, since the original Gamma density has
exponential tails and both polynomials have finite degree.
Pointwise $|f(c+iy)|^2=\prod_j(y^2+t_j^2)\geq\prod_jt_j^2$;
the original polynomial bound GCR29 on the degree-$q$ input
$\chi$ proves
\[
 \prod_{j=0}^{l-1}t_j^2\leq\mathfrak r_\chi\leq\mathscr U_{l,q}.
\tag{GSR7}
\]
Consequently $|\log\mathfrak r_\chi|=O_m(k\log(k+2))$ along
the stated degrees. For example the upper logarithm in GSR7
is bounded by
$l\log(4(q+l)^2+4l^2)$, and the lower logarithm is at least
$-\log4$, since $t_0^2=1/4$ and $t_j^2>1$ for $j\geq1$.
In particular $\log\mathfrak r_\chi/(kq)\to0$.

The four copies of $q\log\beta_k$ cancel with their original
signs. Equations GSR4--GSR6 therefore give
\[
\begin{gathered}
 C_k=\log D_{l,q-1}+\log D_{l,q}-\log\mathfrak r_\chi
                     -\log D_{l,2q-1}-\log D_{l,2q},\\
 \boxed{\quad \mathfrak T_k=C_k+\log R_{2q-1}+\log R_{2q}.\quad}
\tag{GSR8}
\]
Thus the two high-degree determinants in this formula are the
complete original relation determinants.

\subsection{A finite Jacobi realization with the original source metric}

Let $b_n(y)$ and $\gamma_n$ be exactly GCR11, and let
$e_n(y)=b_n(y)/\sqrt{\gamma_n}$. For a positive integer $D$
define the real symmetric matrix $\mathcal J_D$ on coordinates
$0,\ldots,D-1$ by
\[
 (\mathcal J_D)_{a-1,a}=(\mathcal J_D)_{a,a-1}
       =\sqrt{a(a-\tfrac12)}\quad(1\leq a<D),
 \qquad(\mathcal J_D)_{a,a}=0.
\tag{GSR9}
\]
For $P\in\mathcal P_{D-1}$ in the original $S$ coordinate,
write
\[
 P(c+iy)=\sum_{n=0}^{D-1}z_n e_n(y),\qquad
 \mathcal C_D(P)=(z_0,\ldots,z_{D-1})^t .
\tag{GSR10}
\]
This is an explicit linear isometry from the original polynomial
source with its $\sigma$ norm to $\mathbb C^D$ with its Euclidean
norm. Its inverse is the polynomial
$S\mapsto\sum_nz_ne_n((S-c)/i)$. The orthonormal coordinate
frame has not altered $d\sigma$ or its mass $\gamma_0=\sqrt{2\pi}$.
The recurrence proves
$\mathcal C_D(((S-c)/i)P)=\mathcal J_D\mathcal C_D(P)$
whenever $\deg P\leq D-2$.

At a fixed endpoint $N$ put
\[
 D=N+l+1,\qquad
 \Phi_l(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{l-1}(x^2+t_j^2),\qquad
 F_l(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{l-1}(x+it_j).
\tag{GSR11}
\]
Every intermediate product of degree at most $l$ with an input
in $\mathcal P_N$ has degree at most $N+l=D-1$. Applying the
recurrence successively before reaching that last degree gives
the exact multiplication identity
\[
 \mathcal C_D(fP)=i^l F_l(\mathcal J_D)\mathcal C_D(P)
       \quad(P\in\mathcal P_N).
\tag{GSR12}
\]
Since $\mathcal J_D$ is self-adjoint,
$F_l(\mathcal J_D)^*F_l(\mathcal J_D)=\Phi_l(\mathcal J_D)>0$.
This equality concerns the squared norm of the exact degree-$l$
map in GSR12; it does not assert that multiplication by a
degree-$2l$ polynomial has no truncation on every source vector.

For the original relation space put
\[
 Z_N=
 \big(\mathcal C_D(\chi),\mathcal C_D(\chi S),\ldots,
                         \mathcal C_D(\chi S^{r_N-1})\big),\qquad
 B_N=Z_N(Z_N^*Z_N)^{-1/2}.
\tag{GSR13}
\]
At $r_N>0$ its columns are independent: cancellation of the
nonzero monic $\chi$ proves independence of the original
polynomials, and GSR10 is injective. Hence $B_N^*B_N=I_{r_N}$.
The exact relation determinant becomes
\[
 \boxed{\quad R_N=\det\bigl(B_N^*\Phi_l(\mathcal J_D)B_N\bigr).\quad}
\tag{GSR14}
\]
Indeed its denominator in GSR3 is $\det(Z_N^*Z_N)$; its
numerator, by GSR12, is
$\det(Z_N^*\Phi_l(\mathcal J_D)Z_N)$.
This proves GSR14 with the full relation subspace present.

The characteristic polynomial of $\mathcal J_D$ is $b_D$.
Expansion of the tridiagonal determinant along its last row
gives the monic recurrence with initial values $1,y$, exactly
GCR11. Its $D$ eigenvalues $x_{D,i}$ are real and simple.
To prove simplicity, the first coordinate of any eigenvector
determines the second by the first row, and then determines
every subsequent coordinate by the nonzero off-diagonal
recurrence; a zero first coordinate forces the whole vector
to vanish. Each eigenspace thus has dimension one, and
self-adjointness gives a full orthonormal eigenbasis.
Let
\[
 0<\pi_{D,1}\leq\cdots\leq\pi_{D,D}
\]
be the eigenvalues of $\Phi_l(\mathcal J_D)$, with multiplicity.
They are exactly the $D$ positive numbers
$\Phi_l(x_{D,i})$, ordered by $|x_{D,i}|$.
In its orthonormal eigenbasis the Cauchy--Binet formula gives
\[
 R_N=\sum_{\substack{I\subset\{1,\ldots,D\}\\|I|=r_N}}
       w_{N,I}\prod_{i\in I}\pi_{D,i},\qquad
 w_{N,I}\geq0,\quad\sum_Iw_{N,I}=1.
\tag{GSR15}
\]
Here $w_{N,I}$ is the squared determinant of the rows $I$
of the actual matrix $B_N$ in that eigenbasis. The last equality
is Cauchy--Binet applied to $B_N^*B_N=I$.
It follows that the finite spectral bounds are
\[
 s^-_{l,N}:=\sum_{i=1}^{r_N}\log\pi_{D,i}
       \leq\log R_N
       \leq\sum_{i=D-r_N+1}^D\log\pi_{D,i}
                       =:s^+_{l,N}.
\tag{GSR16}
\]
Empty sums are zero. All eigenvalues here come from the explicitly
specified original recurrence matrix; no packet-limit model has
been substituted for it.

\subsection{The actual positive weights and the original mixed determinant}

The weights in GSR15 can be written explicitly, so that its
comparison is tied to the complete original packet. Let $v_i$
be a real unit eigenvector of $\mathcal J_D$ at $x_{D,i}$,
with first coordinate positive, and put
\[
 \omega_{D,i}=\gamma_0(v_i)_0^2>0,\qquad
                    \sum_i\omega_{D,i}=\gamma_0.
\tag{GSR17}
\]
The eigenvector recurrence gives
$(v_i)_n=\sqrt{\omega_{D,i}}\,e_n(x_{D,i})$.
It follows directly from GSR10 that
$v_i^*\mathcal C_D(P)=
\sqrt{\omega_{D,i}}\,P(c+ix_{D,i})$ for every
$P\in\mathcal P_{D-1}$. This proves the evaluation formula
with its original mass, without introducing a probability
normalization of the source.

Order a subset $I$ by its distinct real nodes. The corresponding
minor of $Z_N$ is a product of the evaluation values of $\chi$,
the square roots of $\omega_{D,i}$, and the Vandermonde
determinant of $c+ix_{D,i}$. Thus
\[
 w_{N,I}=
 \frac{\displaystyle
   \prod_{i\in I}\omega_{D,i}|\chi(c+ix_{D,i})|^2
   \prod_{\substack{i<j\\i,j\in I}}(x_{D,j}-x_{D,i})^2}
 {\displaystyle
   \det\operatorname{Gram}_\sigma
               (\chi,\chi S,\ldots,\chi S^{r_N-1})}.
\tag{GSR18}
\]
The absolute value of the Vandermonde phase
$i^{r_N(r_N-1)/2}$ is one. Its original coordinate shift $c$
cancels in the differences, not in the original columns.
Every packet factor in this formula is explicitly
\[
 |\chi(c+ix)|^2
  =\prod_{a,b=0}^k
     \left(((2a-k)\delta)^2+
                    (x-(2b-k)\gamma)^2\right)^{e_k}>0.
\tag{GSR19}
\]
Positivity uses that $2a-k$ is nonzero for this odd $k$.
Thus every weight in GSR18 is strictly positive when $r_N>0$.
The complete multiplicity $e_k$ and every original mixed support
point enter this exact formula.

The weights sum to one because they are squared minors of
an isometric frame. They are coefficients in a finite
determinant identity, not replacement source masses. In
particular the original quadrature weights in GSR17 retain
their total $\sqrt{2\pi}$.

For a direct connection to the complete mixed matrix of GCR26,
let $U_f$ be the full jet multiplication matrix in GCR7,
and let $d_N$ be precisely GCR23. Subtracting the fixed
quotient formula in GCR25 and using GSR4 yields
\[
 \log d_N
     =2\log|\det U_f|-\log D_{l,N}+\log R_N.
\tag{GSR20}
\]
Every matrix in GSR14--GSR18 therefore maps to that same
$2l$ determinant by this exact scalar identity. The
degree-independent unit factor cancels only in the four signed
terms, giving GSR8 and GCR26 with identical values.
No mixed term in the positive factorization GCR24 has been
dropped; GSR20 computes its full determinant.

\subsection{A strictly narrower finite signed enclosure}

The scalar source inequality GCR29 and the determinant
compression argument GCR31--GCR32 also give
\[
 \log D_{l,N}-q\log\mathscr U_{l,N}
    \leq\log R_N\leq r_N\log\mathscr U_{l,N}.
\tag{GSR21}
\]
The lower side follows by applying
$\log\det G_N^f-\log\det G_N^\sigma\leq
q\log\mathscr U_{l,N}$ in GSR4.
The upper side is the direct determinant inequality on the
actual relation space, which has dimension $r_N$.
The pointwise lower bound for $|f|^2$ gives in addition
$\log R_N\geq r_N\sum_j\log t_j^2$.
Define the following entirely finite numbers:
\[
\begin{split}
 L_{l,N}
 &=\max\left\{s^-_{l,N},\
     \log D_{l,N}-q\log\mathscr U_{l,N},\
                       r_N\sum_{j=0}^{l-1}\log t_j^2\right\},\\
 U_{l,N}
 &=\min\left\{s^+_{l,N},\
                         r_N\log\mathscr U_{l,N}\right\}.
\end{split}\tag{GSR22}
\]
All entries are explicit products or eigenvalues of GSR9;
the full original moment in $C_k$ remains exactly GSR5.
Equations GSR8, GSR16 and GSR21 prove
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 C_k+L_{l,2q-1}+L_{l,2q}
       \leq\mathfrak T_k
       \leq C_k+U_{l,2q-1}+U_{l,2q}.
 \quad}\tag{GSR23}
\]
This interval is contained in GCR33. Indeed at each high
endpoint GSR22 includes both bounds used to prove GCR33;
at the low endpoints GSR6 supplies their exact values instead
of the two ranges used there.
Its upper side is strictly smaller for $l\geq1$.
To check this without relying on a spectral approximation,
the high upper choices in GSR22 give
\[
 C_k+U_{l,2q-1}+U_{l,2q}
 \leq A_{q-1}+A_q
       -q\log\mathscr U_{l,2q-1}
       -q\log\mathscr U_{l,2q}
       +X_{l,2q-1}+X_{l,2q}.
\]
In contrast, the upper side of GCR33 replaces
$A_{q-1}+A_q$ by
$q\log\mathscr U_{l,q-1}+q\log\mathscr U_{l,q}$.
Their difference is at least $X_{l,q-1}>0$.
For strict positivity, the row-sum estimate in GCR29 is strict
on the constant input at the first multiplication step:
$\|y\|_\sigma^2/\|1\|_\sigma^2=1/2<4q^2$ at $N=q-1$.
The later factors are positive and their stated upper bounds
remain valid, so the full source inequality has a strictly
smaller Rayleigh quotient on that nonzero vector.
Since all its relative eigenvalues are at most one, its
determinant is strictly smaller than one. This is exactly
$X_{l,q-1}>0$.

\subsection{The complete source and observation maps in the refinement}

No relation kernel has been inferred from the sizes of the
comparison matrices. Its actual coefficient injection is
the map $z\mapsto\chi\sum_{a=0}^{r_N-1}z_aS^a$ in GSR13.
The isometry GSR10 takes that injection to $Z_N$;
multiplication by $f$ takes it, by GSR12, to
$i^lF_l(\mathcal J_D)Z_N$. Its two Grams are exactly the
numerator and denominator of GSR3. Hence GSR14 is a proved
map on the full original source relation.

For the original remainder fibre let
$R_N^f=(H_N^f)^{-1}J_{\chi,N}^*G_N^f$.
The same source minimum argument as GCR14 gives
$J_{\chi,N}R_N^f=I$ and
\[
 \ker(\Lambda J_{\chi,N})
    =\chi\mathcal P_{N-q}\ \mathbin{\perp_{H_N^f}}\
                         R_N^f(\ker\Lambda).
\tag{GSR24}
\]
The first summand is sent to the exact matrix image in the
preceding paragraph, and the second is sent to
$i^lF_l(\mathcal J_D)\mathcal C_D R_N^f(\ker\Lambda)$.
Their orthogonality follows from the source equality GSR12.
The ambient product-jet observation remains
$(0,Y)\mapsto\Lambda\mathcal E_\chi^{-1}U_f^{-1}Y$
from GCR44; the isometry GSR10 and its displayed inverse
make its composition with the finite Jacobi coordinates
explicit. Thus the refinement preserves the full original
unit, nilpotents, source relation and proper observation kernel.

The moving bounds for the same finite spectral products are
proved in the adjoining Jacobi quantile calculation. They
are obtained from the original moving finite matrices,
not from a fixed-packet kernel limit.

\subsection{The resulting moving signed constants}

The complete finite proof JQR1--JQR39, included with this source,
gives an elementary counting law for the same matrices in GSR9.
Define the exact number $a\in(0,2)$ and the exact integral $I$ by
\[
 a\operatorname{arcosh}(2/a)+2\arcsin(a/2)=\pi/2,\qquad
 I=\frac1\pi\int_a^2\log x\,\operatorname{arcosh}(2/x)\,dx.
\tag{GSR25}
\]
Existence and uniqueness of $a$ follow from the strictly
increasing function in JQR13--JQR14. It is the middle absolute
eigenvalue cutoff of the proved limiting counting measure,
not a new parameter of the original quartet.
The positive and negative finite products in GSR16 satisfy
at exactly $N=2q-1,2q$, with $D=N+l+1$, $r_N=N+1-q$,
\[
\begin{split}
 s^+_{l,N}
     &=2lr_N\log D+2lD I+o(lD),\\
 s^-_{l,N}
     &=2lr_N\log D-2lD(1+I)+o(lD).
\end{split}\tag{GSR26}
\]
Here JQR22 is an explicit finite upper-product error;
JQR34 and JQR38--JQR39 give explicit finite full- and
lower-product errors. In particular no lower-tail logarithm
is inferred from weak convergence near a zero eigenvalue.
The auxiliary spectral coordinate $x_{D,i}/D$ is returned
to the original eigenvalue by every factor of $D$ in GSR26.

To verify the moving domains, the two pairs are precisely
\[
 (D,r_N)=(2q+l,q),\quad(2q+l+1,q+1).
\tag{GSR27}
\]
They obey $r_N/D\to1/2$, $l/D\to0$ and
$l\log(2(D+l))/D\to0$, since
$q=e_k(k+1)^2\geq(k+1)^2$ and $q=O_m(k^3)$.
These are the domains required in the fully finite JQR
proof. Both upper products and their complementary ranks
are thereby controlled at these actual degrees.

For explicit cancellation of the growing elementary terms,
GCR35 says
\[
 \log D_{l,N}=2l(N+1)(\log(N+1)-1)+\theta_{l,N+1},
\]
where its displayed bound for $\theta$ is
$O(l^2\log(N+2))$ on these degrees. GSR7 gives
$\log\mathfrak r_\chi=o(lq)$.
Using $N_a+1=q,q+1,2q,2q+1$ in GSR8 yields
\[
 \frac{C_k}{2lq}
          =-2\log q-4\log2+2+o(1).
\tag{GSR28}
\]
For instance replacing $(q+1)\log(q+1)$ by $q\log q$
costs $O(\log(q+1))$ by the mean value theorem; after
division by $q$ this tends to zero. The same reasoning
handles $2q+1$, and the finite $\theta$ errors divided
by $lq$ are $O(l\log q/q)\to0$. Thus the equality
retains, and then cancels, the terms in $\log q$.

The two upper-product expansions in GSR26 give
\[
 \frac{s^+_{l,2q-1}+s^+_{l,2q}}{2lq}
             =2\log q+2\log2+4I+o(1).
\tag{GSR29}
\]
Indeed $D/q\to2$, the two ranks are $q,q+1$, and
$D=2q+O(l)$, so
$\log D=\log(2q)+O(l/q)$.
The lower products instead give
\[
 \frac{s^-_{l,2q-1}+s^-_{l,2q}}{2lq}
             =2\log q+2\log2-4(1+I)+o(1).
\tag{GSR30}
\]
Insert these bounds in GSR8 using GSR16, and then use
$2l/k\to1/2$. The resulting signed conclusion is
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 -1-\log2-2I
 \leq\liminf_{\substack{k\to\infty\\k\equiv1\ (4)}}
                    \frac{\mathfrak T_k}{kq}
 \leq\limsup_{\substack{k\to\infty\\k\equiv1\ (4)}}
                    \frac{\mathfrak T_k}{kq}
 \leq1-\log2+2I.
 \quad}\tag{GSR31}
\]
This is a statement about the actual signed GCR26 value.
The fully finite estimate is GSR23, which is valid also
before any finite JQR cutoff guard holds.

The constants in GSR31 are strictly sharper than those
in GCR39, without relying on a decimal evaluation of $I$.
The counting measure of JQR6 has total mass one and second
moment $2/3$. Its restriction to $|x|\geq a$ has mass $1/2$.
Concavity of $\log$ on this restriction, applied to $x^2$,
therefore gives
\[
 I=\frac12\int_{|x|\geq a}\log x^2\,d\nu(x)
 \leq\frac14\log\left(2\int_{|x|\geq a}x^2\,d\nu(x)\right)
 \leq\frac14\log(4/3).
\tag{GSR32}
\]
This application only averages the explicitly derived spectral
counting law $\nu$; it does not rescale either original Gamma source.
Consequently the upper constant of GSR31 is at most
$1-\tfrac12\log3<1$, and its lower constant is at least
$-1-2\log2+\tfrac12\log3>-1-2\log2$.
GSR25 is the exact value of the sharper constants; no
numerical approximation is needed for these strict improvements.

The original source correction is still
$\Delta_k^\Gamma=\delta_k^\sigma-\mathfrak T_k$ by GCR27.
Using the already proved determinant mass-rate return
$\delta_k^\sigma=o(kq)$ gives
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 -1+\log2-2I
 \leq\liminf_{\substack{k\to\infty\\k\equiv1\ (4)}}
                       \frac{\Delta_k^\Gamma}{kq}
 \leq\limsup_{\substack{k\to\infty\\k\equiv1\ (4)}}
                       \frac{\Delta_k^\Gamma}{kq}
 \leq1+\log2+2I.
 \quad}\tag{GSR33}
\]
The interval in GSR31, like its finite version GSR23,
is an enclosure of the signed value, not its asserted value.
The actual packet weights in GSR18 remain present in GSR15
and GSR20. This proof establishes neither a nonzero leading
value nor a vanishing leading value for that weighted sum;
it retains the sum itself as the complete finite object.

\section{A finite Jacobi calculation for the moving upper spectral product}

The matrices and factors in this calculation have their original coefficients.
For an integer \(D\geq1\), let \(J_D\) be the real symmetric matrix on
\(\mathbb R^D\), with coordinates indexed by \(0,\ldots,D-1\), whose diagonal
is zero and whose two entries joining coordinates \(n-1,n\) are
\[
 a_n=\sqrt{n(n-\tfrac12)},\qquad 1\leq n\leq D-1.
 \tag{JQR1}
\]
Put \(A_D=J_D/D\), with the exact inverse relation \(J_D=D A_D\).
This is an auxiliary coordinate for the finite spectrum.  Every power of
\(D\) is retained, in particular in (JQR23); it does not replace the
original source coordinate \(c=k/2\) or the original source measure.
The eigenvalues of \(A_D\), counted with multiplicity, define
\(\mu_D=D^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^D\delta_{\lambda_j(A_D)}\).
For an integer \(l\geq1\), retain every factor in
\[
 t_j=2j+\tfrac12,\qquad
 \Phi_l(y)=\prod_{j=0}^{l-1}(y^2+t_j^2),\qquad
 B_l=\sum_{j=0}^{l-1}t_j^2
     =\frac{l(16l^2-12l-1)}{12}.
 \tag{JQR2}
\]
All eigenvalues of \(\Phi_l(J_D)\) are positive.  They are ordered by the
absolute values of the corresponding eigenvalues of \(J_D\), because
\(\Phi_l(y)\) is strictly increasing as a function of \(|y|\geq0\).
For \(0\leq r\leq D\), write \(\Pi^+_{D,l,r}\) for the product of its
largest \(r\) eigenvalues.  An empty product is one.

\paragraph{The exact finite walk estimate.}
The following bounds hold for every \(D\geq1\) and integer \(p\geq1\):
\[
 \operatorname{spec}(A_D)\subset[-2,2],\qquad
 \frac1D\operatorname{tr}A_D^{\,2p+1}=0,\qquad
 \left|\frac1D\operatorname{tr}A_D^{\,2p}
       -\frac{\binom{2p}{p}}{2p+1}\right|
 \leq \frac{\binom{2p}{p}(2p^2+3p+1)}D .
 \tag{JQR3}
\]
Indeed, \(0<a_n<n\) and every absolute row sum of \(J_D\) is less than
\(2D\), unless the row sum is zero.  The operator norm bound follows
from the maximum absolute row sum for a real symmetric matrix.  The
diagonal matrix with entries \((-1)^i\), \(0\leq i<D\), conjugates
\(J_D\) to \(-J_D\), giving zero trace for every odd power, including
the first power.

Here is the bound for even powers, including the boundary rows.  Set
\(C_p=\binom{2p}{p}\).  There are exactly \(C_p\) sequences of \(2p\)
nearest-neighbour steps with \(p\) positive and \(p\) negative steps.
Starting at a coordinate \(i\) with \(p\leq i\leq D-1-p\), all these
closed walks stay in the matrix.  An edge used by any such walk has
index \(n\) satisfying \(|n-i|\leq p\).  The elementary inequalities
\[
 n-\tfrac12\leq a_n\leq n,\qquad
 \left|\frac{a_n}{D}-\frac{i}{D}\right|
 \leq\frac{p+\tfrac12}{D}
 \tag{JQR4}
\]
follow by squaring the lower inequality and using \(n\geq1\).
Every factor in a walk product and every comparison factor \(i/D\)
belongs to \([0,1]\).  The telescoping identity for a difference of
products therefore bounds the difference between a walk product and
\((i/D)^{2p}\) by \(p(2p+1)/D\).
There are at most \(2p\) remaining, boundary starting coordinates.
At one such coordinate, both the actual sum of valid walk products
and \(C_p(i/D)^{2p}\) lie in \([0,C_p]\); their difference in absolute
value is at most \(C_p\).  This assertion still applies when
\(D\leq2p\), in which case every row may be a boundary row.  Consequently,
\[

 \frac{\det(Y^*DY)}{A^s\det(Y^*Y)}
 =\det(V^*\mathsf EV)\le1 .}
 \tag{QDC12}
\]
This proves the restriction statement for its original domain
frame, including $s=0$ and $s=n$.

For use with the original polynomial source, let $H_0,H$ be
positive matrices on the same original coefficient space
$\mathcal V=\mathbb C^n$, with $H\preceq AH_0$. Retain a fixed
onto matrix $J:\mathcal V\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal E$ and set
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 D=H_0^{-1/2}HH_0^{-1/2},\qquad L=JH_0^{-1/2},\\
 G_0=(JH_0^{-1}J^*)^{-1},\quad
 G=(JH^{-1}J^*)^{-1},\quad
 R_H=H^{-1}J^*G.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{QDC13}
\]
The coordinate map $b=H_0^{1/2}a$ preserves both original
forms exactly:
\[
 a^*H_0a=b^*b,\qquad a^*Ha=b^*Db,\qquad Ja=Lb.
 \tag{QDC14}
\]
Thus $Q_D=G$, $Q_1=G_0$, and $R_H=H_0^{-1/2}S_D$.
The maps in QDC13--14 prove the claimed correspondence between
the original source and QDC1; no source vector, relation or
target coefficient is discarded. In these original frames,
QDC8 becomes
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 d(H,H_0;A)=n\log A-\log\frac{\det H}{\det H_0}\ge0,\\
 0\le
 r\log A-\log\frac{\det G}{\det G_0}
 \le d(H,H_0;A).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{QDC15}
\]
Here $r=\dim\mathcal E$. For an original injection
$Y_0:\mathbb C^s\hookrightarrow\mathcal V$, the map in QDC12
is $Y=H_0^{1/2}Y_0$. It proves
\[
 0\le s\log A
       -\log\frac{\det(Y_0^*HY_0)}{\det(Y_0^*H_0Y_0)}
 \le d(H,H_0;A).
 \tag{QDC16}
\]
If $Y_0$ spans exactly $\ker J$, its restriction deficit and
the quotient deficit in QDC15 sum exactly to $d(H,H_0;A)$.
Indeed $H_0^{1/2}Y_0(Y_0^*H_0Y_0)^{-1/2}$ is an orthonormal
basis of $\ker L$; substituting this $K$ into QDC10 proves
the statement with every original determinant retained.

\subsection{The four original polynomial quotients}

Retain the original packet, its integer multiplicity $m\ge1$,
and its parameters $\delta,\gamma$ from the full quartet.
Write
\[
 \ell_k=1+k(m-1),\quad q_k=(k+1)^2\ell_k,\quad c_k=k/2,\quad
 \chi_k(S)=\prod_{a,b=0}^k
 \bigl(S-c_k-(2a-k)\delta-i(2b-k)\gamma\bigr)^{\ell_k}.
 \tag{QDC17}
\]
The coefficient space is
$\mathcal E_k=\mathbb C[S]/(\chi_k)$, in its increasing
remainder frame of degrees zero through $q_k-1$.
The source $\mathcal P_N$ retains its increasing power frame
$1,S,\ldots,S^N$ and its literal value $S=c_k+iy$.
For $N\ge q_k-1$ its onto map is the unchanged monic remainder
\[
 J_{k,N}:\mathcal P_N\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal E_k,\qquad
 J_{k,N}P=[P],\qquad
 \ker J_{k,N}=\chi_k\mathcal P_{N-q_k}.
 \tag{QDC18}
\]
The last space is zero when $N=q_k-1$. The full-unit inclusion
$[P]\mapsto U^{\otimes k}[P(s_1+\cdots+s_k)]$ remains the
original subsequent map; QDC18 makes no replacement of $U$,
of its jets, or of the tensor nilpotents.

Let $w_h(y)=|v_h(1/2+iy)|^2/(2\pi)$ be the original
arithmetic source density, with the entire quotient $v_h=g/h$
and $g=2\xi$ from that packet. Put $\alpha=\pi/2$ and
$M_\alpha=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{\alpha y}w_h(y)\,dy>0$.
The two forms used in this calculation are exactly
\[
 \begin{split}
 (H_{k,N})_{ab}
 &=\int_{\mathbb R}\overline{(c_k+iy)}^{\,a}(c_k+iy)^b
                    w_h^{*k}(y)\,dy,\\
 (H_{0,k,N})_{ab}
 &=\int_{\mathbb R}\overline{(c_k+iy)}^{\,a}(c_k+iy)^b
       \frac{|\Gamma(1/4+iy/2)|^2}{2\pi}\,dy ,
 \qquad 0\le a,b\le N .
 \end{split}
 \tag{QDC19}
\]
Thus $H_{0,k,N}=H_N^{\sigma,k}$ is the fixed one-factor Gamma
measure evaluated on the same shifted powers. Its total mass
is $\sqrt{2\pi}$. It is not the $k$-fold Gamma convolution.
The total mass of the first measure is the original $\mu_h^k$.
All moments and the strict positivity of these forms are
those of the original source calculation.

The full source upper comparison has the same scalar at every
degree:
\[
 H_{k,N}\preceq A_kH_{0,k,N},\qquad
 A_k=\frac{C_h}{c_\Gamma}\,k^{p+1}M_\alpha^{\,k-1},
 \quad p=8m-\frac92,\quad c_\Gamma=\sqrt2\,e^{-7/6}.
 \tag{QDC20}
\]
Here $C_h$ is the retained original tilt constant; none of these
constants are absorbed into the measures or coefficient frames.
For these matrices let $D_{k,N}$ be QDC13's exact relative
operator and let
\[
 \begin{split}
 G_{k,N}&=(J_{k,N}H_{k,N}^{-1}J_{k,N}^*)^{-1},\\
 G^\sigma_{k,N}
   &=(J_{k,N}H_{0,k,N}^{-1}J_{k,N}^*)^{-1},\\
 d_{k,N}&=(N+1)\log A_k-\log\det D_{k,N},\\
 b_{k,N}&=q_k\log A_k
                -\log\frac{\det G_{k,N}}{\det G^\sigma_{k,N}}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{QDC21}
\]
The exact map $L_{k,N}=J_{k,N}H_{0,k,N}^{-1/2}$ in
QDC13 proves, separately at each degree and without any
degree-dependent choice of quotient,
\[
 0\le b_{k,N}\le d_{k,N}.
 \tag{QDC22}
\]

For the four specified endpoints, retain their signs and
their source dimensions:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 (N_0,N_1,N_2,N_3)=(q_k-1,q_k,2q_k-1,2q_k),\\
 (\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3)
      =(1,1,-1,-1),\\
 (N_0+1,N_1+1,N_2+1,N_3+1)
      =(q_k,q_k+1,2q_k,2q_k+1).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{QDC23}
\]
Define their original quotient determinant sums
$F_{\rm ar,k}=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\log\det G_{k,N_i}$
and
$F_{\sigma,k}=\sum_i\varepsilon_i\log\det G^\sigma_{k,N_i}$.
Substituting the exact QDC21 equality, not replacing any
of its four deficits by a common unknown error, gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 F_{\rm ar,k}-F_{\sigma,k}
 &=-b_{k,q_k-1}-b_{k,q_k}
                  +b_{k,2q_k-1}+b_{k,2q_k},\\
 -d_{k,q_k-1}-d_{k,q_k}
 &\le F_{\rm ar,k}-F_{\sigma,k}
 \le d_{k,2q_k-1}+d_{k,2q_k}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{QDC24}
\]
The scalar $q_k\log A_k$ cancels because every quotient
has the same dimension $q_k$ and the stated signs sum to zero.
The four source dimensions differ and were retained in
$d_{k,N}$; their scalar factors were not canceled incorrectly.

Here is the exact passage from a source determinant rate to
this signed quantity. Define the literal source-rate remainder
and the literal upper-rate remainder by
\[
 e_{k,N}=\frac{\log\det D_{k,N}}{k(N+1)}-\log M_\alpha,
 \qquad
 \epsilon_k^A=\frac{(p+1)\log k+\log(C_h/c_\Gamma)-\log M_\alpha}{k}.
 \tag{QDC25}
\]
These are definitions, and their relation to the finite
deficit is the identity
\[
 \frac{d_{k,N}}{kq_k}
   =\frac{N+1}{q_k}(\epsilon_k^A-e_{k,N})\ge0.
 \tag{QDC26}
\]
In particular $\epsilon_k^A\to0$. The source determinant asymptotic proved in DMR26,
$\log\det D_{k,N_i}=(N_i+1)k\log M_\alpha+o(k(N_i+1))$
is precisely $e_{k,N_i}\to0$ at each of these four endpoints.
Its use in QDC26 is exact: the dimension multipliers in
QDC23 are at most $2+1/q_k$, so all four
$d_{k,N_i}/(kq_k)$ tend to zero. Substituting this result
into the two sides of QDC24 proves the requested propagation
\[
 \frac{F_{\rm ar,k}-F_{\sigma,k}}{kq_k}\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{QDC27}
\]
The finite inequality QDC24 is independent of any asymptotic.
QDC25--27 specify exactly how the full determinant estimate,
proved in the source determinant calculation, enters the
quotient calculation. This independent calculation does not
replace that estimate by an assumption about quotient
eigenvalues, a fixed-degree limit, or four diagonal entries.

\subsection{The actual boundary and its retained kernel}

Fix the original onto observation
$\Lambda_k:\mathcal E_k\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal B_k$,
with its actual image as codomain, and its fixed kernel
inclusion $I_k:\mathcal K_k\hookrightarrow\mathcal E_k$.
This includes the period and monodromy observation with the
entire $U^{\otimes k}$ factor already present. Put
$r_k=\dim\mathcal B_k$ and $t_k=q_k-r_k$.
For either of the two quotient Grams $G$ in QDC21 define
\[
 H^K(G)=I_k^*GI_k,\quad
 Q^B(G)=(\Lambda_kG^{-1}\Lambda_k^*)^{-1},\quad
 S^B(G)=G^{-1}\Lambda_k^*Q^B(G).
 \tag{QDC28}
\]
The exact section identities QDC2--3 apply to $\Lambda_k$:
its section is $G$-orthogonal to $I_k$, and every vector
of $\mathcal E_k$ decomposes uniquely into a kernel vector
and this section's lift. In particular
$[I_k,S^B(G)]^*G[I_k,S^B(G)]
 =\operatorname{diag}(H^K(G),Q^B(G))$.

Choose once a coefficient right inverse $S_*$ of $\Lambda_k$,
independent of $N$ and of which source form is used.
The difference $S^B(G)-S_*$ has image in $\mathcal K_k$,
so is uniquely $I_kT_G$ for a matrix $T_G$. Therefore
\[
 \det[I_k,S^B(G)]=\det[I_k,S_*],\qquad
 \det H^K(G)\det Q^B(G)
        =|\det[I_k,S_*]|^2\det G.
 \tag{QDC29}
\]
This proves the exact frame cancellation in a ratio of the
two sources as well as in the four endpoint sum.

Minimizing $H_{k,N}\preceq A_kH_{0,k,N}$ on each identical
fibre of $J_{k,N}$ proves
$G_{k,N}\preceq A_kG^\sigma_{k,N}$ directly from QDC3.
Use this pair of forms in QDC15--16 with the fixed
$\Lambda_k$ and $I_k$. Define
\[
 \begin{split}
 b^K_{k,N}
 &=t_k\log A_k-
      \log\frac{\det H^K(G_{k,N})}
                    {\det H^K(G^\sigma_{k,N})},\\
 b^B_{k,N}
 &=r_k\log A_k-
      \log\frac{\det Q^B(G_{k,N})}
                    {\det Q^B(G^\sigma_{k,N})}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{QDC30}
\]
Both are nonnegative by the exact restriction and quotient
inequalities. QDC29 proves their exact sum, and QDC22 bounds it:
\[
 b^K_{k,N}+b^B_{k,N}=b_{k,N}\le d_{k,N}.
 \tag{QDC31}
\]
For either superscript $X=K$ or $X=B$, its arithmetic-minus-
reference four-endpoint determinant sum is consequently
\[
 \Delta F^X_k
   =-b^X_{k,q_k-1}-b^X_{k,q_k}
                   +b^X_{k,2q_k-1}+b^X_{k,2q_k},
 \qquad
 -d_{k,q_k-1}-d_{k,q_k}\le\Delta F^X_k
      \le d_{k,2q_k-1}+d_{k,2q_k}.
 \tag{QDC32}
\]
Its common scalar cancels with the same four signs, with
dimension $t_k$ or $r_k$, respectively. The original complete
sum satisfies the exact equality
$F_{\rm ar,k}-F_{\sigma,k}=\Delta F^K_k+\Delta F^B_k$.
By the original-source determinant limit DMR26 and the exact propagation QDC25--27,
each of $\Delta F^K_k/(kq_k)$ and
$\Delta F^B_k/(kq_k)$ tends to zero separately.
Neither the kernel nor a mixed block in its minimum section
has been deleted.

These identities control the rate relative to the specified
fixed one-factor Gamma source. They do not assign a sign to
QDC24 or QDC32, identify that reference with the original
$k$-fold Gamma endpoint, or prove an RH contradiction.
In particular, $o(kq_k)$ is the scale established by
QDC25--27; a smaller scale does not follow by renaming
the four deficits.

% END EXACT REQUIRED PROOF QDC

 \tag{OCF2}
\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically, first by $a$, then by $b$.
The order is used only for the exact coefficient elimination.
Set $\mathcal B_d=0$ for $d<0$. Multiplication satisfies

their difference is divisible by $t_{++}t_{--}-t_{+-}t_{-+}$,
using $A^n-B^n=(A-B)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A^{n-1-j}B^j$.

pair, so it is a sum of such differences. The reverse inclusion

\subsection{The complete homogeneous ideal, with quadratic generators}

$\mathscr P_Z=\mathbb C[Z_{a,b,d}:a,b\in\{0,1\},0\le d\le d_m]$

\[

\[

 \tag{OMG9}
\]

indices with sum $a$, independently $k$ binary second indices with
sum $b$, and $k$ integers in $[0,d_m]$ with sum $D$; the last
choice follows by filling successive slots up to $d_m$. Combining
the three lists into rows gives the required preimage monomial.
Distinct displayed target monomials are linearly independent.

Let $\mathfrak t_m$ be generated by every quadratic binomial
\[
 Z_{a,b,d}Z_{a',b',d'}-Z_{c,e,f}Z_{c',e',f'}
 \quad\text{with}\quad
 a+a'=c+c',\quad b+b'=e+e',\quad d+d'=f+f',
 \tag{OMG10}
\]
where every index belongs to its original range. Repeated variables
are allowed. Then
\[
 \boxed{\ker\Phi_m=\mathfrak t_m,\qquad
           \mathscr P_Z/\mathfrak t_m\simeq R_m.}
 \tag{OMG11}
\]
Here is a complete ideal proof. Each displayed quadratic has zero
image. Two degree-$k$ monomials have the same image exactly when
the sums of their first indices, second indices and third indices
agree. Regard their $k$ factors temporarily as labelled rows. Align
the first indices with the target list by pairwise swaps of first
indices, keeping each row's other indices fixed. Each swap is an
OMG10 relation. Next align the second indices by the same operation,
keeping the aligned first indices fixed. Finally, if the third
indices differ from their target list, choose a row below its target
and a row above its target. Increase the former third index by one
and decrease the latter by one. These entries stay in $[0,d_m]$
because their target entries do; the total sum is unchanged and the
sum of absolute deviations decreases by two. This terminates at
the target list. Each transfer is another OMG10 relation. Thus the
difference between any two monomials with the same image is a sum
of multiples of the quadrics, by telescoping the successive monomial
differences. Labels only specify the sequence of polynomial maps;
the products are the original commutative monomials throughout.
For any polynomial in $\ker\Phi_m$, collect its coefficients by
their target monomial. Each such coefficient sum is zero by target
monomial independence. Subtracting one chosen monomial in each
group expresses that whole group as a linear combination of the
proved monomial differences. This proves the reverse inclusion for
all degrees and hence the entire ideal equality.

Every degree-$k$ original curve monomial has the function
\[

of $b$ and equality of imaginary parts gives equality of $a$.

$\sum_{a,b}P_{a,b}(w)e^{\omega_{a,b}w}=0$, with
$\deg P_{a,b}\le kd_m$. Fix a pair and apply
$\prod_{(a',b')\ne(a,b)}(\partial_w-\omega_{a',b'})^{kd_m+1}$.

nilpotent and the constant is nonzero. The surviving polynomial
is therefore zero. Repeating this for every pair proves independence.

Fourier inversion and a contour shift within $|\operatorname{Im}x|<\pi/2$.
In particular it includes the exact masses $M_1=\sqrt{2\pi}$ and
$M_k=(2\pi)^{k/2}$ and exponential domination on every smaller strip.
The original real monic polynomials satisfy
\[
\begin{gathered}
 p_0=1,\quad p_1=y,\quad
 p_{d+1}=yp_d-d(b_s+d-1)p_{d-1},\\
 \sum_{d\ge0}\frac{p_d(y)}{d!}z^d
      =(1+z^2)^{-b_s/2}e^{y\arctan z},\qquad
 h_d^{(s)}=\|p_d\|^2=M_s d!(b_s)_d.
\end{gathered}\tag{AKS16}
\]
The generating formula follows by differentiating in $z$. To check the
normalization directly, integrate the product of two generating
functions at small real $z,w$. AKS15 and the cosine addition identity
give $M_s(1-zw)^{-b_s}$. Taking any finite pair of derivatives at zero,
justified by the stated exponential domination, gives orthogonality and
the norms in AKS16. Thus the leading phase in
$u_d(S)=p_d((S-c)/i)/\sqrt{h_d^{(s)}}$ is exactly $i^{-d}$.
The same generating function agrees with NIST DLMF 18.23.7 after the
original parameter rescaling; it is derived here from the supplied
recurrence, not substituted for it.

List the original roots
$\omega_\nu=(\lambda_{a,b}-c)/i$ in lexicographic order, repeating each
exactly $e$ times, and put
\[
 P(y)=i^{-q}\chi(c+iy)=\prod_{\nu=1}^q(y-\omega_\nu),\qquad
 \Phi:[f(y)]\mapsto[f((S-c)/i)].
 \tag{AKS17}
\]
The inverse is substitution $S=c+iy$, and
$P((S-c)/i)=i^{-q}\chi(S)$. This is an exact algebra isomorphism, including
the complete confluent orders; there is no monomial comparison divisor.
Let $C_s$ have columns $[u_0],\ldots,[u_{q-1}]$. Its nonzero determinant
is $i^{-q(q-1)/2}\prod_{d<q}(h_d^{(s)})^{-1/2}$. Define
\[
 v_j=C_s^{-1}[u_{q+j}],\qquad
 \mathsf K_j=I_q+\sum_{a=0}^{j-1}v_av_a^*,\qquad 0\le j\le q+1.
 \tag{AKS18}
\]
Parseval in the low-degree original orthonormal polynomial basis proves
\[
 \|v_j\|_2^2=
 \frac{\|\operatorname{rem}_P p_{q+j}\|_{m_{0,s}}^2}
      {M_s(q+j)!(b_s)_{q+j}}.
 \tag{AKS19}
\]
This is the full norm of the actual remainder, not a diagonal entry of
an approximated quotient Gram.

\subsection{Newton interpolation with all roots and their orders}
For $0\le a<q$ define $N_a(y)=\prod_{\nu=1}^a(y-\omega_\nu)$, with
$N_0=1$. For every complex $v$, the unique entire-function remainder is
\[
 \operatorname{rem}_P(e^{vy})
   =\sum_{a=0}^{q-1}[\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{a+1}]e^{v\cdot}\ N_a(y),
 \qquad
 \left|[\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{a+1}]e^{v\cdot}\right|
       \le\frac{|v|^a}{a!}e^{R|v|}.
 \tag{AKS20}
\]
Here divided differences at repeated nodes mean Hermite divided
differences, not evaluation with a zero denominator.

A proof covering the confluent case is useful. On the standard
$a$-simplex with barycentric coordinates $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{a+1}$,
\[
 [\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{a+1}]e^{v\cdot}
       =v^a\int_{\Delta_a}e^{v\sum_\nu\theta_\nu\omega_\nu}\,d\theta.
\]
The integral of $\prod\theta_\nu^{n_\nu}$ is
$\prod n_\nu!/(a+\sum n_\nu)!$, as follows by iterated integration of
integer beta integrals. Expanding the exponential therefore gives
$\sum_{n\ge0}v^{a+n}h_n(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_{a+1})/(a+n)!$.
For monomials, the divided difference of $y^{a+n}$ is exactly $h_n$:
this follows by multiplying the geometric series
$\prod(1-\omega_\nu z)^{-1}$ and the Newton division recurrence.
It is a polynomial identity in the nodes and so also holds at repeated
nodes. This proves the integral formula. Iterated Newton division for
polynomials, followed by the convergent exponential series, proves the
first equality in AKS20, including every required derivative.
Finally the simplex has volume $1/a!$ and
$|\sum\theta_\nu\omega_\nu|\le R$, proving its stated bound.

For any $0<t<\pi/2$, put $\tau=2/t$. Positivity of every term of the
cosh series in AKS15 gives
\[
 \|y^a\|_{m_{0,s}}
 \le\sqrt{M_s}(\cos t)^{-b_s/2}\tau^a a!.
\]
Indeed its square is at most
$M_s(\cos t)^{-b_s}(2a)!t^{-2a}$ and
$(2a)!\le4^a(a!)^2$. Expanding the \emph{whole} Newton polynomial, then
using $|e_j(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_a)|\le\binom ajR^j$, proves
\[
\begin{split}
 \|N_a\|_{m_{0,s}}
 &\le\sqrt{M_s}(\cos t)^{-b_s/2}
        \sum_{j=0}^a\binom ajR^{a-j}\tau^j j!\\
 &=\sqrt{M_s}(\cos t)^{-b_s/2}\tau^a a!
           \sum_{n=0}^a\frac{(R/\tau)^n}{n!}\\
 &\le\sqrt{M_s}(\cos t)^{-b_s/2}\tau^a a!e^{R/\tau}.
\end{split}\tag{AKS21}
\]
There are no omitted polynomial coefficients. Combining AKS20--21 gives
for every complex $v$
\[
 \|\operatorname{rem}_P(e^{vy})\|_{m_{0,s}}
 \le\sqrt{M_s}(\cos t)^{-b_s/2}e^{R(|v|+t/2)}
                       \sum_{a=0}^{q-1}(2|v|/t)^a.
 \tag{AKS22}
\]

\subsection{Cauchy extraction in the actual Gamma generating function}
Fix $0<z<1$ and write $a_z=\operatorname{arctanh}z$.
For $|w|=z$ the defining power series gives
$|\arctan w|\le a_z$ and $|1+w^2|\ge1-z^2$.
Apply the literal finite-dimensional remainder map to AKS16 and use
Cauchy's formula for its $d$th coefficient. The norm triangle inequality
on that circle and AKS22 give
\[
\begin{split}
 \frac{\|\operatorname{rem}_P p_d\|_{m_{0,s}}}{d!}
 \le{}&z^{-d}(1-z^2)^{-b_s/2}\sqrt{M_s}(\cos t)^{-b_s/2}\\
 &\mathrel{}\times e^{R(a_z+t/2)}
                    \sum_{a=0}^{q-1}(2a_z/t)^a.
\end{split}\tag{AKS23}
\]
Cauchy's formula is legitimate for the finite remainder vector: its
entries are holomorphic for $|w|<1$ by the actual matrix generating
identity OPG7. The source norm is taken only after this finite-vector
identity; there is no unjustified integral of a nonintegrable generating
function on the large circle.

Substitution of AKS23 into AKS19 retains the factorial denominator and
cancels the two occurrences of the original mass, giving
\[
 \boxed{\ 
 \|v_j\|_2^2\le\frac{d!}{(b_s)_d}z^{-2d}
 [\cos t(1-z^2)]^{-b_s}e^{2R(a_z+t/2)}
 \left[\sum_{a=0}^{q-1}(2a_z/t)^a\right]^2,
 \quad d=q+j.\ }
 \tag{AKS24}
\]
Adding the \emph{complete} rank-one positive matrices in AKS18 now proves
$\mathsf K_j\preceq \mathcal Z_{s,j}I_q$ after setting $z=4/5$ and $t=t_q$.
Indeed $a_{4/5}=\log3$, $1-z^2=9/25$, and $\cos t_q=\sin(1/q)$, so
the exact scalar obtained is AKS3. The high index $j=q+1$ includes the
original polynomial of degree $2q$.

There is also a root-by-root finite refinement. Put
$\mu_{s,d}=\int y^{2d}dm_{0,s}$,
$R_a=\max_{\nu\le a+1}|\omega_\nu|$, and
\[
\begin{gathered}
 B_{s,a}^{\rm root}=\sum_{d=0}^a
     |e_{a-d}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_a)|\sqrt{\mu_{s,d}},\\
 J_s^{\rm root}(z)=\frac{(1-z^2)^{-b_s}}{M_s}
 \left[\sum_{a=0}^{q-1}\frac{a_z^a}{a!}e^{a_zR_a}
                      B_{s,a}^{\rm root}\right]^2.
\end{gathered}\tag{AKS25}
\]
Replace the scalar multiplying
$d!z^{-2d}/(b_s)_d$ in AKS24 by $J_s^{\rm root}(z)$ to get a valid
sharper bound, by the same proof before AKS21 is relaxed. Every moment
is exactly $M_s(2d)![w^{2d}](\cos w)^{-b_s}$. Thus this refinement keeps
every actual root coefficient and a finite original moment formula.
AKS21 bounds it by the explicit scalar in AKS24. The proof never replaces
the source determinant by a product of diagonal moments: AKS24 is a
full-vector operator bound, and the next step restricts the inverse of
the full covariance.

\section{The four original kernel Grams and the evaluated scale}
\label{sec:AKS-volume}

The original orthonormal source map at degree $q+j-1$ is
$C_s[I_q,v_0,\ldots,v_{j-1}]$. Its minimum lift of $C_sx$ is
$[I_q,v_0,\ldots,v_{j-1}]^*\mathsf K_j^{-1}x$. It has that image and is
orthogonal to the full relation kernel, so Pythagoras proves
\[
 G_{q+j-1}^{(s)}=C_s^{-*}\mathsf K_j^{-1}C_s^{-1},\qquad
 H_j:=H_{K,q+j-1}^{(s)}=T_s^*\mathsf K_j^{-1}T_s,\quad T_s=C_s^{-1}I.
 \tag{AKS26}
\]
This verifies the source-minimum step in the coefficient determinant
AKS13--14. Neither a cross block nor any original relation is removed.

Since $I_q\preceq\mathsf K_j\preceq \mathcal Z_{s,j}I_q$, inversion and compression
give $\mathcal Z_{s,j}^{-1}H_0\preceq H_j\preceq H_0$, where $H_0=T_s^*T_s$.
Define $d_j=-\log\det(H_0^{-1/2}H_jH_0^{-1/2})$. Congruence and all
$r$ eigenvalues give
\[
 0=d_0\le d_1\le\cdots\le d_{q+1},\qquad
 0\le d_j\le r\mathcal L_{s,j},\qquad
 F_K^{(s)}=d_q+d_{q+1}-d_1.
 \tag{AKS27}
\]
The identity uses precisely the four endpoints in AKS2.
In particular it proves AKS4, as well as the sharper interval
\[
 \boxed{\quad d_1\le F_K^{(s)}\le
             r(\mathcal L_{s,q}+\mathcal L_{s,q+1})-d_1.\quad}
 \tag{AKS28}
\]
For a directly calculable expression for its lower endpoint set
$V=\|v_0\|^2$ and
$\theta=v_0^*T_s(T_s^*T_s)^{-1}T_s^*v_0$. Then
\[
 0\le\theta\le V,\qquad
 d_1=\log\frac{1+V}{1+V-\theta}.
 \tag{AKS29}
\]
Indeed the inverse of $I+v_0v_0^*$ is
$I-v_0v_0^*/(1+V)$; take its full compressed determinant. For $r=0$
set $\theta=d_1=0$. In GMB/OPR notation $V=t_0$ and $V-\theta=\xi_0$,
so this is exactly the first original section-corrected kernel increment,
not an independently chosen kernel observation.

Here is an evaluated finite remainder for AKS6. Put
\[
\begin{gathered}
 a_\infty=\frac{4\log3}{\pi},\qquad
 c_0=\log\frac{25\log3}{4\pi}>0,\\
 E_{s,q}(R)=\log2+\frac4{\pi-2/q}
  +\frac{s}{2}\log\frac{25\pi q}{18}
  +2R\left(\log3+\frac\pi4\right)\\
 \hspace{23mm}+\log((q+1)(4q+1))-2\log(a_\infty-1).
\end{gathered}\tag{AKS30}
\]
Then for both source orders, every $q\ge36$, and the same actual kernel,
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mathcal L_{s,q},\mathcal L_{s,q+1}\le2c_0q+E_{s,q}(R),\qquad
 0\le F_K^{(s)}\le4rc_0q+2rE_{s,q}(R).
 \quad}\tag{AKS31}
\]
To verify every factor, $b_s\ge1/2$ gives
\[
 \frac{d!}{(b_s)_d}\le\frac{4^d}{\binom{2d}{d}}\le2d+1.
\]
The last inequality uses that the central binomial is the largest of the
$2d+1$ positive coefficients whose sum is $4^d$. Thus the sum in AKS3
is at most $(q+1)(4q+1)(5/4)^{4q}$. Also
$\mathfrak s_q\le \mathfrak a_q^q/(a_\infty-1)$ and
\[
 2q\log \mathfrak a_q\le2q\log a_\infty+\frac4{\pi-2/q},\qquad
 \sin(1/q)\ge\frac2{\pi q}.
\]
The first follows from $-\log(1-x)\le x/(1-x)$ at $x=2/(\pi q)$;
the second is the chord bound for sine on $[0,\pi/2]$.
Use $t_q\le\pi/2$ in the remaining exponential. The order-$q$ terms
combine to
$4q\log(5/4)+2q\log a_\infty=2c_0q$.
The upper bound for the logarithm of the added positive scalar is
positive, so $\log(1+e^x)\le\log2+\max(0,x)$ proves the first bound in
AKS31. AKS28 proves the second.

On the original simple family $q=(k+1)^2$, $R=O_h(k)$ and
$r=8k-16$. Consequently $E_{1,q}(R)=O_h(k+\log q)$ and
$E_{k,q}(R)=O_h(k\log q)$. Dividing AKS31 by $kq$ proves AKS6, with
$32c_0=\kappa_*$. In fact the fixed-source upper bound is
\[
 F_K^{(1)}\le(32k-64)c_0q+(16k-32)E_{1,q}(R),
 \tag{AKS32}
\]
whose explicit second term is $O_h(k^2)$. The tensor-source version has
an $O_h(k^2\log q)$ upper remainder. These are remainders of upper
bounds, not assertions about the actual signed error or leading value.
The proof is uniform in all the period parameters in the stated domain:
no norm or condition number of a period matrix occurs in AKS30.

\paragraph{The precise earlier loss.}
OKV15 had already retained
$\|v_j\|^2\le q^22^{6q}(2D_*q)^{2d}/(d!(b_s)_d)$, $d=q+j$.
Replacing its denominator by $1/2$ caused the old $q\log q$ exponent.
Even without AKS20--24 one obtains the valid repair
\[
 \|\mathsf K_{q+1}\|\le
 1+(q+1)q^22^{6q}\frac{(4D_*q)^{4q}}{(4q)!},\qquad D_*\ge3.
 \tag{AKS33}
\]
Here $d!(b_s)_d\ge(2d)!/4^d$ and the remaining factorial ratio increases
up to $d=2q$ for $D_*\ge3$. The elementary inequality
$\log n!\ge n\log n-n+1$ already makes the logarithm of AKS33 $O_h(q)$.
The Newton calculation strengthens this repair to the packet-independent
limsup constant AKS5, while retaining $R$ in its finite remainder.


\paragraph{Exact enclosure of the displayed numerical ceiling.}
For $x>1$ and $z=(x-1)/(x+1)$ the integrated geometric series gives
\[
 0\le \log x-2\sum_{j=0}^{39}\frac{z^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
      \le\frac{2z^{81}}{81(1-z^2)}.
\]
For $0<x<1$, the alternating sum through $j=39$ for $\arctan x$
has error between zero and $x^{81}/81$. The tangent addition formula,
with the angle in $(0,\pi/2)$, proves
$\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$: the tangent of
$4\arctan(1/5)-\arctan(1/239)$ is exactly one. Use the resulting
rational lower and upper bounds for $\pi$ and for $\log3$, then apply
the first displayed bound to the two endpoints of
$25\log3/(4\pi)$. Multiplication by $32$ gives, with outward decimal
rounding, the interval
\[
 \kappa_*\in[25.0207809764994871,\ 25.0207809764994872].
\]
The accompanying rational-arithmetic implementation checks these
inequalities by integer cross multiplication, rather than a floating-point
logarithm. This proves the less finely rounded strict interval AKS5.

\section{The finite conductor inverse in the two original Gamma norms}
\label{sec:AIE}

Retain AKJ12--25 and the complete OCF conductor coefficient polynomial.
Thus $m=1$, $k=4l+1\ge9$, $q=(k+1)^2$, $0<\delta<1/2$,
$\gamma>2$, and the original period belongs to the proved five-orbit
locus. Its fixed $4$ by $4$ matrix $\mathsf H$ determines the four
quadrics and all $81$ coefficients $a_{rs}$ of their full product.
They remain the same coefficients as the tensor degree $k$ varies.
Put
\[
 b_{rs}=4+(2r-8)\delta+i(2s-8)\gamma,\quad
 \mu_j=\sum_{r,s=0}^8a_{rs}b_{rs}^j,\quad
 v=\min\{j:\mu_j\ne0\}\le80.
 \tag{AIE1}
\]
The existence and bound for $v$ are the full distinct-node Vandermonde
argument of AKJ13. Throughout, $0\le D\le q-1$ denotes the polynomial
degree cutoff. Every norm below is the original Gamma norm of source
order $s\in\{1,k\}$, with
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 b=s/2,\quad M=(2\pi)^{s/2},\quad h_n=M n!(b)_n,\\
 \varphi_n=p_n/\sqrt{h_n},\quad w_n=n!/(b)_n,
 \quad \|p\|_{s,c}=\|p(c+iy)\|_{m_{0,s}}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{AIE2}
\]
The centre $c$ is displayed wherever it changes. No source order,
source mass, coefficient, or period is assigned a replacement value.

\subsection{A coefficient-controlled disk for the literal finite symbol}

The exact symbol used in AKJ14 and AKJ17 is
\[
 B_q(z)=1+\sum_{j=v+1}^{q-1}
                \frac{v!\mu_j}{j!\mu_v}z^{j-v}.
 \tag{AIE3}
\]
The sum is empty if its lower index exceeds its upper index. Define
the positive, original-data constants
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A_*^{\rm abs}=\sum_{r,s}|a_{rs}|,\qquad
 B_*^{\rm sh}=\max_{r,s}|b_{rs}|,\qquad
 C_v=\frac{A_*^{\rm abs}(B_*^{\rm sh})^v}{|\mu_v|},\\
 R_0=\frac{1}{B_*^{\rm sh}}
       \min\left\{1,\frac{v+1}{2\mathrm e C_v}\right\},
 \quad \rho_0=\tanh R_0.
 \end{gathered}\tag{AIE4}
\]
Here $A_*^{\rm abs}>0$, $B_*^{\rm sh}\ge4$, $C_v\ge1$,
$R_0>0$, and $0<\rho_0<1$. The superscripts distinguish these
constants from the original conductor polynomial and from every
earlier radius or pivot coefficient. The exact moment $\mu_v$,
including any cancellation in it, remains in the denominator.

For every $|z|\le R_0$ one has
\[
 |B_q(z)-1|
 \le \frac{v!}{|\mu_v|}
       \sum_{j=v+1}^{q-1}\frac{|\mu_j|}{j!}|z|^{j-v}
 \le C_v\frac{B_*^{\rm sh}|z|}{v+1}
                    \exp(B_*^{\rm sh}|z|)
 \le\frac12.
 \tag{AIE5}
\]
To prove the middle inequality, use
$|\mu_j|\le A_*^{\rm abs}(B_*^{\rm sh})^j$, write
$j=v+1+h$, and apply
$v!/(v+1+h)!\le1/((v+1)h!)$. Summation of the exponential
series gives the displayed bound. Definition AIE4 gives
$B_*^{\rm sh}R_0\le1$ and
$C_v B_*^{\rm sh}R_0/(v+1)\le1/(2\mathrm e)$, proving
the last inequality. The first upper bound in AIE5 retains every
individual finite moment and may be used directly for a larger
verified radius. The explicit $R_0$ proves a positive disk for
every actual coefficient chart; no uniform lower bound for
$|\mu_v|$ over varying periods is asserted.

The analytic function
\[
 F_q(z)=\frac1{B_q(-i\arctan z)}
          =\sum_{a=0}^\infty f_{q,a}z^a
 \tag{AIE6}
\]
is well defined on a neighbourhood of the closed disk
$|z|\le\rho_0$, and
$|F_q(z)|\le2$ there. Indeed the power series of $\arctan$
gives $|\arctan z|\le\operatorname{arctanh}|z|\le R_0$;
AIE5 gives $|B_q(-i\arctan z)|\ge1/2$. Compactness gives
an open neighbourhood with nonzero denominator. Cauchy's coefficient
formula therefore proves
\[
 f_{q,0}=1,\qquad |f_{q,a}|\le2\rho_0^{-a}
                    \quad(a\ge1).
 \tag{AIE7}
\]
Although the literal symbol $B_q$ changes with $q$, the disk and its
bound depend only on the original fixed conductor and shifts.

\subsection{The exact coefficient map and its norm}

Let $\mathcal P_D$ denote the polynomials in $y$ of degree at most

\[
 L_s\varphi_0=0,\qquad
 L_s\varphi_n=\sqrt{\frac{w_n}{w_{n-1}}}\,\varphi_{n-1}

 \tag{AIE8}
\]
Its powers have exactly the entries
$L_s^a\varphi_n=\sqrt{w_n/w_{n-a}}\varphi_{n-a}$ for

AKJ21 gives the polynomial identity
$\partial_y=\arctan L_s$, with every power above degree $D$

the chain rule is
$\mathcal C_c\partial_S\mathcal C_c^{-1}=-i\partial_y$.

\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal C_c B_q(\partial_S)^{-1}\mathcal C_c^{-1}
   &=F_q(L_s),\\

   &=\sum_{a=0}^n f_{q,a}
                     \sqrt{\frac{w_n}{w_{n-a}}}\,\varphi_{n-a}.
 \end{split}\tag{AIE9}
\]
For proof, evaluate the analytic power-series identity
$B_q(-i\arctan z)F_q(z)=1$ in the nilpotent matrix $L_s$.
All relevant coefficients are finite, so multiplication is an exact
finite polynomial identity. This also proves that AIE9 is the same

Define the exact weight ratio and the resulting bound
\[
 \begin{split}

                         \sqrt{\frac{w_n}{w_m}},\\

            \left(1+2\sum_{a=1}^{D}\rho_0^{-a}\right)
 \le \frac{2\alpha_{D,s}}{1-\rho_0}\rho_0^{-D}.
 \end{split}\tag{AIE10}
\]
Every absolute row sum and every absolute column sum of AIE9 is at
most $\alpha_{D,s}\sum_{a=0}^D|f_{q,a}|$. Cauchy--Schwarz in each
row followed by the column bound proves that the operator norm is
at most this number; AIE7 gives $N_{D,s}$. It follows that, at every
unchanged centre $c$,
\[
 \|B_q(\partial_S)^{-1}p\|_{s,c}
                \le N_{D,s}\|p\|_{s,c}.
 \tag{AIE11}
\]
When $s=k$, $b=k/2\ge1$ and
$w_n/w_{n-1}=n/(b+n-1)\le1$, so $\alpha_{D,k}=1$.
When $s=1$, the same ratio is greater than one, so
$\alpha_{D,1}=\sqrt{D!/(1/2)_D}$; for $D\ge1$, the exact

\[

       +\log\frac{2\alpha_{D,s}}{1-\tanh R_0}

\]
For the fixed original quartet and period, $q=(k+1)^2$ and

its constants explicitly retain the actual $\mu_v$.

\subsection{The infinite symbol differs by an exact low-degree map}

To record precisely the truncation in AIE3, define the entire function

No coefficient in these polynomials is replaced. The exact orbit

\subsection{The original Segre coefficient isomorphism}

For $d\geq0$ let $\mathcal B_d$ be the space of biforms of
bidegree $(d,d)$ in $(z_0,z_1)$ and $(w_0,w_1)$. Its ordered basis is
\[
 e_{ab}^{(d)}=z_0^a z_1^{d-a}w_0^b w_1^{d-b},
 \qquad 0\leq a,b\leq d.
 \tag{OCF2}
\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically, first by $a$, then by $b$.
The order is used only for the exact coefficient elimination.
Set $\mathcal B_d=0$ for $d<0$. Multiplication satisfies
$e_{ab}^{(d)}e_{ij}^{(e)}=e_{a+i,b+j}^{(d+e)}$.
The original substitution is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 t=(z_0w_0,z_0w_1,z_1w_0,z_1w_1)^T,\qquad x=\mathsf Ht,\\
 \mathscr P_d=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]_d,\qquad
 \psi_d:\mathscr P_d\longrightarrow\mathcal B_d,\quad
 f\longmapsto f(\mathsf Ht).
 \end{gathered}\tag{OCF3}
\]
The induced map
$R_d=\mathscr P_d/(Q\mathscr P_{d-2})\longrightarrow\mathcal B_d$
is an isomorphism. Here is a coefficient proof with the given
orientation. For each $(a,b)$, choose an integer
$h$ between $\max(0,a+b-d)$ and $\min(a,b)$. The monomial
$t_{++}^{h}t_{+-}^{a-h}t_{-+}^{b-h}t_{--}^{d-a-b+h}$ maps
to $e_{ab}^{(d)}$, proving surjectivity. Two monomials with
the same pair differ in their exponent vectors by an integer
multiple of $(1,-1,-1,1)$. After removing their common monomial,
their difference is divisible by $t_{++}t_{--}-t_{+-}t_{-+}$,
using $A^n-B^n=(A-B)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A^{n-1-j}B^j$.
A polynomial in the kernel has coefficient sum zero within every
pair, so it is a sum of such differences. The reverse inclusion
in the kernel follows by direct substitution. The invertible
substitution $x=\mathsf Ht$ then gives exactly the asserted kernel.
Thus these maps preserve multiplication as well as every grading.

Write the full conductor restriction as
\[
 A=\psi_8(\mathcal A)
     =\sum_{r=0}^8\sum_{s=0}^8 a_{rs}e_{rs}^{(8)}\ne0.
 \tag{OCF4}

\subsection{Every leading-coefficient case gives an exact strip frame}

Let $(r_*,s_*)$ be the lexicographically largest pair for which
$a_{r_*s_*}\ne0$, and put $a_*=a_{r_*s_*}$. This is an
actual nonzero coefficient of OCF4. For $d\geq8$ define
\[
 \begin{split}
 P_d&=\{(r_*+i,s_*+j):0\leq i,j\leq d-8\},\\
 E_d^{\rm strip}&=\{0,\ldots,d\}^2\setminus P_d,\qquad
 W_d=\mathbb C^{E_d^{\rm strip}}.
 \end{split}\tag{OCF5}
\]
For $0\leq d<8$ put $P_d=\varnothing$,
$E_d^{\rm strip}=\{0,\ldots,d\}^2$ and use the same definition
of $W_d$; for $d<0$ put $W_d=0$. Let
$S_d:W_d\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^{(d+1)^2}$ insert zeros in
the positions $P_d$. All coefficient columns below use OCF2.

The following finite elimination defines
$N_d:\mathbb C^{(d+1)^2}\to W_d$ and, for $d\geq8$,
$V_d:\mathbb C^{(d+1)^2}\to\mathbb C^{(d-7)^2}$.
Starting with the complete input biform $f$, traverse all
$(i,j)\in\{0,\ldots,d-8\}^2$ in decreasing lexicographic order.
At the step $(i,j)$, let $c$ be the current coefficient at
$(r_*+i,s_*+j)$, record $b_{ij}=c/a_*$, and replace the current
biform by
\[
       f_{\rm current}-b_{ij}A e_{ij}^{(d-8)}.
 \tag{OCF6}
\]
At completion take the coefficients on $E_d^{\rm strip}$ as
$N_df$ and take $(b_{ij})$ as $V_df$. If $d<8$, $N_d$ is the
identity and $V_d$ is the zero map into the zero space.
The exact multiplication matrix $M_{A,d}$ gives
\[
 S_dN_d+M_{A,d}V_d=I,\qquad
 N_dS_d=I_{W_d},\qquad
 \ker N_d=A\mathcal B_{d-8}.
 \tag{OCF7}
\]
To prove these identities, the largest term of
$A e_{ij}^{(d-8)}$ is $a_*e_{r_*+i,s_*+j}^{(d)}$;
every other term is strictly smaller in the same lexicographic
order. Therefore each step zeros its designated position without
altering an earlier zero. Summing all subtractions gives the
first identity. Input supported on the strip produces zero
coefficients at every elimination step, giving the second.
Finally, the leading term of $Ab$, for a nonzero homogeneous
biform $b$, is the product of the two leading terms and belongs
to $P_d$. Indeed every other product is smaller in the additive
lexicographic order. Thus
$A\mathcal B_{d-8}\cap S_dW_d=0$. The first identity now proves
the kernel formula, the uniqueness of the decomposition, and all
three identities in OCF7. All operations are linear in the input;
their coefficients are explicit rational expressions in the
original $a_{rs}$ with powers of the displayed $a_*$ as denominators.
The polynomial $A$ itself remains the full polynomial OCF4.

\[
 \mathcal B_d/(A\mathcal B_{d-8})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }W_d,

 \begin{cases}(d+1)^2,&0\leq d<8,\\16d-48,&d\geq8.

coefficient cases have been included. At the first original

\subsection{Twenty-five fixed invariant monomials generate all degrees}

\[
 G_e=\{\nu\in\mathbb N^4:|\nu|=e,
                   \nu_1+2\nu_2+3\nu_3+4\nu_4\equiv0\pmod5\},
 \quad 1\leq e\leq5,\qquad G=\bigcup_{e=1}^5G_e.
 \tag{OCF9}
\]
Here $G_1$ is empty. The complete remaining lists, in the original
$x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ order, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
e&G_e\\\hline
2&(0,1,1,0),(1,0,0,1)\\
3&(0,0,2,1),(0,1,0,2),(1,2,0,0),(2,0,1,0)\\

\subsection{Exact multiplication on the strip and the invariant recursion}

Let $\mathcal L=\mathcal B/(A\mathcal B)$, a graded algebra.
For $\nu\in G_e$ and $d\geq e$ define
\[
 m_{\nu,d}:W_{d-e}\longrightarrow W_d,
 \qquad m_{\nu,d}=N_d M_{f_\nu}S_{d-e}.
 \tag{OCF14}
\]
Here $M_{f_\nu}$ is the exact coefficient convolution:
\[
       (M_{f_\nu}S_{d-e}v)_{ab}

with out-of-range indices giving zero.

 \overline J_0=\mathbb C\cdot1,\qquad

   \sum_{\substack{\nu\in G_e\\2\leq e\leq5,\ e\leq d}}

\[

\subsection{Exact ranks, a finite pivot atlas, and the original quotient map}

For $d\geq0$ put
\[
 d_0(d)=\frac{\binom{d+3}{3}+4\epsilon_d}{5},\qquad

\]

\subsection{The actual primary, unit, period and Fourier coefficient map}
Retain the original full-order quartet and every original period
parameter. Write
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \alpha_{\epsilon,\eta}=\tfrac12+\epsilon\delta+i\eta\gamma,
 \quad\epsilon,\eta\in\{-1,1\},\quad0<\delta<\tfrac12,\quad\gamma>2,\\
 m\ge1,\quad d_m=m-1,\quad n=4m,\quad N=4m+1,\quad
 h(z)=\prod_{\epsilon,\eta}(z-\alpha_{\epsilon,\eta})^m,\\
 E_h=\mathbb C[z]/(h),\quad A_h=M_z,\quad

\end{gathered}\tag{OMG1}
\]
The last inequalities follow from the stipulated complete original

of orders $0,\ldots,m-1$ at all four roots. Let
$\mathcal E_{\rm prim}:\mathbb C^{4m}\to E_h$ send its coordinate
$(\alpha,d)$ to the original primary element $\varepsilon_\alpha
(z-\alpha)^d$, $0\le d<m$. Explicitly its representative is
\[
 E_{\alpha,d}(z)=\operatorname{rem}_h\left[
 h_\alpha(z)\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}
       \frac{(h_\alpha^{-1})^{(j)}(\alpha)}{j!}(z-\alpha)^{j+d}
                                      \right],\quad
 h_\alpha=h/(z-\alpha)^m.
\]
The Taylor inverse is defined since $h_\alpha(\alpha)\ne0$.
It gives the idempotent one on its own primary factor and zero
on the others. The four coprime factors therefore prove that
$\mathcal E_{\rm prim}$ is an isomorphism and include every
nilpotent degree. In this basis the full matrix of $U$ is
\[
 U_{\rm prim;\alpha,a;\alpha,d}
 =\begin{cases}v_h^{(a-d)}(\alpha)/(a-d)!,&a\ge d,\\0,&a<d,
   \end{cases}\qquad
 \det U=\prod_\alpha v_h(\alpha)^m\ne0.
 \tag{OMG2}
\]
Other primary blocks are zero. Inverting its constant coefficient
plus its nilpotent part by the finite geometric series proves
invertibility with all derivatives retained.

Keep the original $u\ne0$ and its logarithm branch, the primitive
$\Phi_h'=h$, $\Phi_h(0)=0$, the outward rays $\ell_j$ of angles
$(\arg u+\pi+2\pi j)/N$, and $\Gamma_j=-\ell_0+\ell_j$.
The exact period and Fourier maps are
\[
\begin{gathered}
 (\Pi[P])_j=\int_{\Gamma_j}e^{\Phi_h(z)/u}
                     \operatorname{rem}_hP(z)\,dz,\quad1\le j\le n,\\
 \zeta=e^{2\pi i/N},\quad F_{jt}=\zeta^{jt}-1,\quad

\end{gathered}\tag{OMG3}
\]
The full original period theorem PDE/OPG gives the convergence and
invertibility of $\Pi$ on these representatives. The Fourier inverse
follows directly from
$\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\zeta^{-tj}(\zeta^{sj}-1)=N\mathbf1_{t=s}$.
It is the same literal cyclic matrix as OCS4, including its inverse
powers in the original average. Its inherited Gram is
$F^*F=N(I_n+\mathbf1\mathbf1^*)$, as expansion of its entries gives.

Define the exact diagonal map and coefficient matrix
\[
\begin{gathered}
 D_m^{\rm jet}=\operatorname{diag}\left(i^{-d}/d!\right)_{\alpha,\,0\le d<m},
 \qquad \mathsf H_m=F^{-1}\Pi U\mathcal E_{\rm prim}D_m^{\rm jet},\\

  =\frac{i^{-d}}{d!}\sum_{a=d}^{m-1}
     \left[\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^{n}\zeta^{-tj}

                  \frac{v_h^{(a-d)}(\alpha)}{(a-d)!}.
\end{gathered}\tag{OMG4}

This is exactly OCS13, now regarded as one square matrix. All

\[

      \left(\prod_\alpha v_h(\alpha)^m\right)

Set $\omega_{\epsilon,\eta}=\eta\gamma-i\epsilon\delta$ and let

\subsection{The complete homogeneous ideal, with quadratic generators}
Use binary indices $a,b\in\{0,1\}$ for
$\epsilon=2a-1$, $\eta=2b-1$. Let
$\mathscr P_Z=\mathbb C[Z_{a,b,d}:a,b\in\{0,1\},0\le d\le d_m]$
with each variable of degree one. Define the algebra map
\[
 \Phi_m:\mathscr P_Z\longrightarrow
        \mathbb C[X_0,X_1,Y_0,Y_1,T_0,T_1],\qquad
 Z_{a,b,d}\longmapsto X_aY_bT_0^{d_m-d}T_1^d.
 \tag{OMG7}
\]
Its image is the complete diagonal graded algebra
\[
 R_m=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}
  \mathbb C[X_0,X_1]_k\otimes\mathbb C[Y_0,Y_1]_k
                              \otimes\mathbb C[T_0,T_1]_{kd_m}.
 \tag{OMG8}
\]
Indeed a basis monomial of its degree-$k$ component is
\[
 X_0^{k-a}X_1^aY_0^{k-b}Y_1^bT_0^{kd_m-D}T_1^D,
       \quad0\le a,b\le k,\quad0\le D\le kd_m.
 \tag{OMG9}
\]
It is a product of $k$ images in OMG7: choose $k$ binary first
indices with sum $a$, independently $k$ binary second indices with
sum $b$, and $k$ integers in $[0,d_m]$ with sum $D$; the last
choice follows by filling successive slots up to $d_m$. Combining
the three lists into rows gives the required preimage monomial.
Distinct displayed target monomials are linearly independent.

Let $\mathfrak t_m$ be generated by every quadratic binomial
\[
 Z_{a,b,d}Z_{a',b',d'}-Z_{c,e,f}Z_{c',e',f'}
 \quad\text{with}\quad
 a+a'=c+c',\quad b+b'=e+e',\quad d+d'=f+f',
 \tag{OMG10}
\]
where every index belongs to its original range. Repeated variables
are allowed. Then
\[
 \boxed{\ker\Phi_m=\mathfrak t_m,\qquad
           \mathscr P_Z/\mathfrak t_m\simeq R_m.}
 \tag{OMG11}
\]
Here is a complete ideal proof. Each displayed quadratic has zero
image. Two degree-$k$ monomials have the same image exactly when
the sums of their first indices, second indices and third indices
agree. Regard their $k$ factors temporarily as labelled rows. Align
the first indices with the target list by pairwise swaps of first
indices, keeping each row's other indices fixed. Each swap is an
OMG10 relation. Next align the second indices by the same operation,
keeping the aligned first indices fixed. Finally, if the third
indices differ from their target list, choose a row below its target
and a row above its target. Increase the former third index by one
and decrease the latter by one. These entries stay in $[0,d_m]$
because their target entries do; the total sum is unchanged and the
sum of absolute deviations decreases by two. This terminates at
the target list. Each transfer is another OMG10 relation. Thus the
difference between any two monomials with the same image is a sum
of multiples of the quadrics, by telescoping the successive monomial
differences. Labels only specify the sequence of polynomial maps;
the products are the original commutative monomials throughout.
For any polynomial in $\ker\Phi_m$, collect its coefficients by
their target monomial. Each such coefficient sum is zero by target
monomial independence. Subtracting one chosen monomial in each
group expresses that whole group as a linear combination of the
proved monomial differences. This proves the reverse inclusion for
all degrees and hence the entire ideal equality.

Every degree-$k$ original curve monomial has the function
\[
 w^D\exp\{[(2b-k)\gamma-i(2a-k)\delta]w\}
       \quad(0\le a,b\le k,\ 0\le D\le kd_m).
 \tag{OMG12}
\]
The frequencies are distinct: equality of real parts gives equality
of $b$ and equality of imaginary parts gives equality of $a$.
To prove independence with all polynomial powers, suppose
$\sum_{a,b}P_{a,b}(w)e^{\omega_{a,b}w}=0$, with
$\deg P_{a,b}\le kd_m$. Fix a pair and apply
$\prod_{(a',b')\ne(a,b)}(\partial_w-\omega_{a',b'})^{kd_m+1}$.
This kills every other summand. On its surviving polynomial each
factor is $\partial_w+(\omega_{a,b}-\omega_{a',b'})$, invertible
on the space of degree at most $kd_m$ because differentiation is
nilpotent and the constant is nonzero. The surviving polynomial
is therefore zero. Repeating this for every pair proves independence.

Thus the full homogeneous ideal of the original primary curve is
exactly $\mathfrak t_m$: a homogeneous polynomial restricts to zero
if and only if its coefficient sums at every target monomial OMG9
are zero. In particular
\[
 \boxed{\dim R_{m,k}=(k+1)^2[1+k(m-1)]=q_k,
 \quad\ker\{\mathscr P_{Z,k}\to\operatorname{Hol}(\mathbb C),
                      f\mapsto f(z(w))\}=\mathfrak t_{m,k}.}
 \tag{OMG13}
\]
This statement concerns the homogeneous ideal, equivalently the
projective closure of $[z(w)]$. Every one of its degrees has been
computed, including degree zero. No assertion about a different
nonhomogeneous affine ideal is used.

\subsection{The projective model and its complete chart inverses}
For $m\ge2$, the morphism
\[
 (\mathbb P^1)^3\longrightarrow\mathbb P^{4m-1},\qquad
 ([X_0:X_1],[Y_0:Y_1],[T_0:T_1])

 Z_{a,b,d}^{d_m}=Z_{a,b,0}^{d_m-d}Z_{a,b,d_m}^{d}

In the actual Fourier coordinates let
